title: Krishna's Dawn Oil Bath
hookLine: the Diwali oil bath before sunrise remembers Krishna's victory over Narakasura; in Hindu practice the body is readied for the sacred
carry: the body is readied for the sacred
tomorrow: how hard should the body be pushed?

lines: HAVE YOU HAD YOUR GANGA BATH?
cards: Before sunrise on one Diwali morning, in many homes in South and western India, nobody gets to sleep in. An elder warms sesame oil and rubs it into everyone's hair and shoulders.
Then a hot bath in the dark, new clothes, and the first firecracker down the street. In Tamil homes, people greet each other that morning with a question: have you had your Ganga bath?
There's a story behind that oil, and a teaching behind the story.

teach.b: The story is Krishna and Narakasura. In the Bhagavata Purana, Naraka is a demon king who has stolen the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and locked away thousands of captive women.
Krishna flies against him on Garuda, with his wife Satyabhama beside him, breaks the fortress, kills Naraka and sets the captives free.
In the version many families tell, Krishna came home at dawn, dusty from the fight, and was given an oil bath.

teach.h: ABHYANGA SNAN: THE DAWN OIL BATH
teach.b: So on Naraka Chaturdashi, one of Diwali's days, and in Tamil Nadu Deepavali itself, families do the same: abhyanga snan, the oil bath before sunrise. Here's the teaching under it.
In Hinduism, caring for the body belongs to worship, not apart from it. Hindus bathe before puja. The Yoga Sutras list shaucha, cleanliness, first among the five observances, the niyamas.
A clean, tended body is how you come before God. Ayurveda's daily routine says the same in a physician's voice.

teach.h: SHAUCHA: THE BODY READIED FOR GOD
teach.b: The Charaka Samhita compares oiling the body to oiling a clay pot, a piece of leather, a cart's axle: each holds up to use when it's oiled, and so does the body.

teach.h: A POT, A HIDE, AN AXLE
teach.b: Today, that changes what self-care means. A grandmother oiling a child's hair on a Sunday night isn't doing a beauty routine.

She's passing down a way of treating the body as worth tending, the way you'd clean a lamp before lighting it. One plain note: oil doesn't suit every skin or every condition; the practice is fitted to the person.

how: On Naraka Chaturdashi, the morning before the main Diwali night, many Hindu families in South and western India take an oil bath before sunrise, abhyanga snan, remembering Krishna's victory over Narakasura; Hindus bathe before puja, and in many homes an elder oils children's hair as a regular practice.

games.q: it's Diwali morning, still dark, and an elder is warming the oil. what's the oil bath about?
o: a beauty routine before the photos.
readying the body for a sacred day, the way Krishna was bathed after defeating Naraka.

games.why: in Hindu practice the body is tended before you come before God: a bath before puja, and on this morning, oil first, the way the story says Krishna was bathed.

practice: Rub your palms together until they're warm, then press slowly from wrist to elbow, then the shoulders, the back of the neck and the crown of the head, the way an elder oils a child's hair.
If you can, splash a little water on your face.
Many Hindus say a short verse while bathing that calls the sacred rivers, Ganga, Yamuna and the rest, into the water; if you pray, you can do the same, and if you don't, just feel the water as care.

wordCard.voice: The daily routine. In many Hindu homes it can begin with oil before sunrise: abhyanga, care for a body being readied for the sacred.

orig.note: Sanskrit abhyanga: oiling and rubbing the body, part of the classical daily routine.
